title: Real-Time: Polling, SSE, WebSockets
subtitle: Watch one chat message reach a user who never asked for it, using four different ways to let a server speak first.
learn: Why plain HTTP cannot push, and how short and long polling fake it
How Server-Sent Events and WebSockets keep one connection open
When to pick polling, SSE or WebSockets
Why connection gateways are stateful and what that does to scaling
How a message crosses gateways through a pub/sub bus, and what happens when a gateway dies

steps.title: The server has news, the client is silent
steps.body: Alice sends Bob a chat message. The server now holds something Bob wants, but HTTP only works one way: a client asks, the server answers. A server cannot start a conversation on its own. So how does Bob's screen update without him refreshing? Throughout this lesson we assume 100,000 connected users.
steps.idea: Plain HTTP is request/response, so real-time needs a trick or a different protocol.
steps.caption: Bob is idle; the news is on the server.

steps.title: Ask again every few seconds
steps.body: The simplest fix: Bob's app asks "anything new?" every 5 seconds. It works with any server and cache. But 100,000 users polling every 5 s is 20,000 requests per second, almost all returning nothing. And a message waits on average half the interval, about 2.5 s, before Bob sees it. Each poll is a short-lived HTTP request, not a held-open socket.
steps.idea: Short polling is trivially simple but wastes requests and adds delay equal to half the poll interval.
steps.caption: Most polls come back empty.

steps.title: Ask, and the server waits
steps.body: With long polling the server does not answer an empty poll. It holds the request open, often up to 30 seconds, and replies when something arrives. Bob's app then asks again. Between replies there is a gap, so each poll carries a last-seen id and the server replays anything missed. Delay is about a network trip; idle traffic falls to roughly 100,000 / 30 = 3,300 requests per second, though each message pays for a new request.
steps.idea: Long polling gives near-instant delivery over plain HTTP by parking the request until there is news.
steps.caption: The request is held, then answered at once.

steps.title: Server-Sent Events: one long download
steps.body: Server-Sent Events (SSE) make that held response permanent. Bob opens one GET with Accept: text/event-stream, and the server keeps writing small text events into it. EventSource reconnects on its own and sends Last-Event-ID so the server can resume. It is one-way and text-only, which fits feeds and notifications. EventSource cannot set headers, so authenticate with a cookie or short-lived token. The client can still send data with normal POSTs. Use HTTP/2, since HTTP/1.1 browsers allow only about 6 connections per origin, and make sure proxies do not buffer the stream.
steps.idea: SSE is a one-way push stream over ordinary HTTP with built-in reconnect and resume.
steps.caption: One open response; events flow down it.

steps.title: WebSockets: a two-way pipe
steps.body: A WebSocket starts as an HTTP request with an Upgrade header. The server answers 101 Switching Protocols and the same TCP connection becomes a full-duplex channel. Both sides now send small frames at any time, each with only 2 to 14 bytes of header. Delivery is as fast as SSE, about one network trip; the gain is two-way traffic. Unlike EventSource, the browser WebSocket API does not reconnect or resume for you, so your code must. That suits chat input, games and collaborative editing, where the client talks as much as the server does.
steps.idea: WebSockets upgrade one HTTP connection into a bidirectional message channel with tiny per-message overhead.
steps.caption: Upgrade handshake, then frames both ways.

steps.title: The gateway remembers who is connected
steps.body: Open connections make servers stateful. Gateway B holds Bob's socket in memory, and a request cannot reach Bob except through that process. Each idle connection costs roughly 10 to 50 KB of memory (a rule of thumb), so 100,000 connections is a few GB, and a tuned box can hold far more. Scaling means adding gateways and spreading connections across them. A load balancer only places new connections, so use least-connections routing and expect a freshly added gateway to start empty.
steps.idea: A connection lives on one specific gateway, so you cannot simply send Bob's message from any server.
steps.caption: Bob is attached to Gateway B only.

steps.title: Delivering across gateways
steps.body: Alice is on Gateway A, Bob on Gateway B. A gateway is the server process that terminates client connections. The chat service first saves the message to a durable store. Gateway A then publishes it to a pub/sub bus, because simple buses (for example Redis Pub/Sub) are often at-most-once and offer no replay. Every subscriber of the channel gets a copy, so Gateway B, which holds Bob's socket, writes the message down it. A reconnecting client catches up from the store.
steps.idea: Persist first, then publish: gateways share messages through a pub/sub bus and a durable store backs up the lossy fast path.
steps.caption: Save first, then A to bus to B to Bob.

steps.title: A gateway dies
steps.body: Gateway B crashes, or is redeployed. Its 50,000 sockets drop at the same instant. If all reconnect within about a second, that is a 50,000 req/s burst, a thundering herd that queues on the survivors and pushes delay toward a second. Clients should wait a random, growing delay (exponential backoff with jitter) and send their last seen message id to resume. Planned deploys should drain: stop accepting, then close sockets gradually.
steps.idea: Connections are fragile, so clients must reconnect with jitter and resume from a message id.
steps.caption: Gateway B fails; clients rush to reconnect.

steps.title: Choosing the tool
steps.body: Use short polling when updates are rare and caching matters, such as a job status check. Use SSE for one-way streams like notifications, prices or live logs. Use WebSockets when the client sends often and latency matters, such as chat, games or shared cursors. Whatever you pick, send a heartbeat every 20 to 30 seconds, because proxies and load balancers cut idle connections, often after 60 s.
steps.idea: Pick the simplest option that matches your direction of traffic, and always heartbeat.
steps.caption: Same message, four transports, different costs.

steps.title: From asking to being told
steps.body: HTTP cannot push, so short polling asks often and long polling parks the question. SSE keeps a one-way stream, and WebSockets give a two-way channel. Open connections pin users to a gateway, so messages cross gateways through a pub/sub bus, and clients must reconnect with backoff and resume. Durable queues and event logs, which can back this bus, have their own lessons.
steps.idea: Real-time is a held-open connection plus a way to route messages to the gateway that owns it.
steps.caption: Connections at the edge, a bus in the middle.

quiz.q: 100,000 users short-poll every 10 seconds. Roughly how many requests per second does the server see, and what is the average delivery delay?
quiz.why: 100,000 / 10 s = 10,000 requests per second. A message arrives at a random point in the interval, so the average wait is half of it, 5 s.

quiz.q: A live stock ticker only sends prices from server to browser and must reconnect automatically after Wi-Fi drops. Which is the best fit?
options: Long polling with a 5 s timeout
quiz.why: Traffic is one-way, which is exactly what SSE does. EventSource reconnects and resumes with Last-Event-ID built in, so WebSockets add complexity without a benefit.

quiz.q: Alice is on Gateway A and Bob on Gateway B. Why can't Gateway A just write to Bob directly?
options: Bob's socket exists only in Gateway B's memory
The load balancer blocks gateway-to-gateway traffic
Gateways may only talk to the database
quiz.why: A connection is held by one process. Gateway A has no handle for it, so the message must reach Gateway B, usually through a pub/sub bus.

quiz.q: A gateway holding 50,000 sockets restarts and all clients reconnect instantly, overloading the other gateways. What is the standard defence?
options: Switch every client to short polling
Reconnect with exponential backoff plus random jitter
quiz.why: Jitter spreads reconnects over time and backoff slows repeated tries, so the herd arrives gradually instead of as one spike.

quiz.q: A WebSocket works on your laptop but drops after exactly 60 seconds of silence in production. The most likely cause?
options: Browsers cap WebSocket age at 60 s
An idle timeout on a proxy or load balancer closing quiet connections
The server ran out of ports
quiz.why: Intermediaries close connections that carry no traffic. Periodic ping or heartbeat frames every 20 to 30 seconds keep them open.

cheatsheet.def: Client asks on a timer. Simple and cache-friendly, but wasteful when idle, and delay averages half the interval.
Server holds the request until data exists or a timeout (about 30 s), then client re-asks. Low delay over plain HTTP.
One long HTTP response of text events, server to client only. Auto-reconnect and Last-Event-ID resume are built into EventSource.
HTTP Upgrade (101) turns the connection into a full-duplex frame channel. Best when both sides send often.
A server that holds open sockets in memory. Needs a way to route messages to the gateway owning each user.
Gateways subscribe to channels for their users; a publisher reaches every subscribed gateway without knowing who is where.
Retry after a random, growing delay so mass reconnects do not stampede. Pair with a last-seen id to resume.
Small periodic ping (every 20-30 s) that stops proxy idle timeouts and reveals dead peers early.
